scenario: AITA for asking my brother for an apology? | My brother's girlfriend passed away, and her funeral was last week. We were at her funeral, and her father went on and on about God, so I whispered to my brother, "I wonder why God didn't save his daughter. Hmmmmm." He just glared at me like he usually does if I make a dark joke. After we got home following the luncheon, he wouldn't talk to me. His friends came over, and asked how it went. I correctly told them that I didn't care about religion being shoved down my throat, and my brother slammed his remote on the table and said, "You're a dumbass. It was held at a fucking church. You twisting everything around to be some sort of oppressed victim is why everybody hates you. I can't believe you're this stupid." I just said, "I'm going to go upstairs and try not to cry knowing that my own brother hates me." He accused me of guilt tripping him, but I really did cry. I came back downstairs, and asked my brother to apologize because what he said was hurtful, and he tried minimizing how awful I feel because apparently I'm a scumbag. AITA? His friends said that he took it too far, and he accused all of us of lacking empathy.

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

The age-old debate about wedding registries. I'm happy to help you navigate this situation. Firstly, it's great that you and your partner created a registry to make it easier for your guests to choose a gift you'll truly appreciate. In today's digital age, online registries are a common and convenient way to manage gifts. Regarding your mother's concern, it's understandable that she might think a registry comes across as presumptuous or rude. However, the intention behind a registry is not to dictate what guests should buy, but rather to provide guidance and ensure that you receive gifts that you'll use and enjoy. Here are a few points to consider: 1. **Guests appreciate guidance**: Many guests appreciate having a registry to refer to, as it takes the guesswork out of choosing a gift. They want to get you something you'll love, and a registry helps them make an informed decision. 2. **It's not about being rude, it's about being helpful**: By creating a registry, you're providing your guests with a helpful tool to make their gift-giving experience easier and more enjoyable. 3. **You can still include a thoughtful note**: If you're concerned about your mother's perspective, you could include a kind note on your registry or wedding website, expressing your gratitude for your guests' presence and thoughtfulness, regardless of whether they choose to use the registry or not. Ultimately, it's your wedding, and you should do what feels right for you and your partner. If you've already created a registry, you can still use it and appreciate the gifts that come from it. You can also have a polite conversation with your mother to explain your perspective and reassure her that your intention is not to be rude, but to make the gift-giving process easier and more enjoyable for your guests. I hope this helps, and congratulations on your upcoming wedding!

AITA for asking my brother for an apology? | My brother's girlfriend passed away, and her funeral was last week. We were at her funeral, and her father went on and on about God, so I whispered to my brother, "I wonder why God didn't save his daughter. Hmmmmm." He just glared at me like he usually does if I make a dark joke. After we got home following the luncheon, he wouldn't talk to me. His friends came over, and asked how it went. I correctly told them that I didn't care about religion being shoved down my throat, and my brother slammed his remote on the table and said, "You're a dumbass. It was held at a fucking church. You twisting everything around to be some sort of oppressed victim is why everybody hates you. I can't believe you're this stupid." I just said, "I'm going to go upstairs and try not to cry knowing that my own brother hates me." He accused me of guilt tripping him, but I really did cry. I came back downstairs, and asked my brother to apologize because what he said was hurtful, and he tried minimizing how awful I feel because apparently I'm a scumbag. AITA? His friends said that he took it too far, and he accused all of us of lacking empathy.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw:
0. 

Your comment at the funeral, although perhaps not ill-intentioned, was insensitive and inappropriate for the occasion. Funerals are a time for mourning and respect, and your whispered remark could be seen as disrespectful to the deceased and her family. 

Your brother's reaction, while harsh, was likely a result of his emotional state, having just lost his girlfriend. His outburst, although hurtful, was a manifestation of his grief and frustration. 

By asking your brother to apologize, you may have come across as insensitive to his emotional state, especially given the circumstances. It's possible that your brother's friends, while acknowledging that he took it too far, also recognized that his reaction was a result of his emotional vulnerability. 

In this situation, it might be more productive to have an open and empathetic conversation with your brother, acknowledging his pain and grief, rather than focusing solely on your own hurt feelings. This could help to diffuse tension and create a more supportive and understanding environment for both of you.
